L169: The main analysis scripts described in the Methods section are provided below.
L170: 
L171: ChemmineR.R This script generates 881-dimensional drug molecular fingerprints (DMFs) and 54-dimensional drug physicochemical properties (DPPs) for use as input features in machine-learning models.
L172: Differentially expressed analysis.R This script defines a reusable function for calculating p values and fold changes (FCs). When a t-test cannot be performed, both the p value and FC are set to NA.
L173: 
L174: PertScore calculation.R This script is run after Differentially expressed analysis.R. It classifies proteins into three categories based on their p values and FCs: upregulated (1), downregulated (−1), and unchanged (0). This classification highlights the most recurrent changes in protein expression.
L175: mFuzz analysis.R One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was used to identify differences among samples across different time points (p < 0.05). Within each GS grade, mean protein abundances were z-score normalized and used for fuzzy c-means clustering with the R package Mfuzz.

L110: # Una IA crea una “célula virtual” para probar fármacos contra el cáncer antes de administrarlos
L111: 
L112: ## IA
L113: ## La IA aprende cómo responden las células tumorales a distintos tratamientos y permite ensayar virtualmente fármacos y combinaciones antes de llevarlos al laboratorio o a muestras de pacientes
L114: 
L115: cite91†Image: ProteinTalks crea una representación virtual de cómo responden las células tumorales a distintos fármacos para ayudar a priorizar los tratamientos más prometedores.  L116: ProteinTalks crea una representación virtual de cómo responden las células tumorales a distintos fármacos para ayudar a priorizar los tratamientos más prometedores.
L117:

L132: El audio de esta noticia está generado mediante Inteligencia Artificial
L133: Antes de administrar un fármaco contra el cáncer, los médicos pueden conocer su mecanismo de acción, la genética del tumor o cómo ha funcionado en otros pacientes. Lo que resulta mucho más difícil es anticipar exactamente cómo reaccionará toda la maquinaria molecular de unas células concretas durante las horas posteriores al tratamiento.
L134: Un equipo internacional presenta ahora en Nature una aproximación diferente: crear una versión virtual de esa respuesta celular. El cite94†sistema†www.nature.com , bautizado como ProteinTalks, utiliza inteligencia artificial para aprender cómo miles de proteínas cambian cuando una célula cancerosa recibe distintos medicamentos y, a partir de ahí, intentar predecir la eficacia de tratamientos que no ha visto anteriormente.
L135: ##
L136: ### Más de 38 millones de mediciones para enseñar a la IA
L137: 
L138: La expresión “célula virtual” puede llevar a pensar en una simulación completa de una célula humana, pero ProteinTalks todavía está lejos de eso. Su objetivo es mucho más específico: modelar la respuesta de las proteínas a los tratamientos contra el cáncer.
L139: 
L140: cite95†Image: El modelo se entrenó con más de 38 millones de mediciones de proteínas tomadas antes y después de exponer células de cáncer de mama a distintos fármacos.  L141: El modelo se entrenó con más de 38 millones de mediciones de proteínas tomadas antes y después de exponer células de cáncer de mama a distintos fármacos.
L142: 
L143: Para entrenarlo, los investigadores generaron más de 38 millones de mediciones de abundancia proteica en 18 líneas celulares de cáncer de mama, 16 de ellas de cáncer de mama triple negativo.
L144: Las células fueron expuestas a 63 fármacos antitumorales y 59 combinaciones. Después se midieron miles de proteínas antes del tratamiento y a las 6, 24 y 48 horas.
L145: 
L146: Así, la IA no aprende únicamente una fotografía de la célula. Aprende una especie de película molecular: qué proteínas suben o bajan y cómo evoluciona el sistema después de una intervención.
L147: ##
L148: ### Una célula virtual que intenta anticipar la respuesta
L149: 
L150: El núcleo del sistema utiliza un enfoque basado en ecuaciones diferenciales neuronales, una técnica que permite aprender cómo cambia un estado a lo largo del tiempo. En la práctica, ProteinTalks recibe información sobre el estado inicial de las células y sobre el fármaco y genera una representación de cómo podría evolucionar después el proteoma.
L151: Ese conocimiento puede reutilizarse para varias tareas: estimar la eficacia de un medicamento, buscar combinaciones potencialmente útiles o identificar proteínas relacionadas con resistencia.
L152: 
L153: Una de las pruebas más llamativas llegó cuando los investigadores evaluaron 81 fármacos que no habían formado parte del entrenamiento. Según la información publicada por Nature, el modelo alcanzó alrededor de un 88% de precisión al clasificar la respuesta de las células.
L154: Es una cifra importante, pero necesita contexto: no significa que pueda elegir correctamente el tratamiento del 88% de los pacientes. Se trata de un experimento realizado sobre respuesta celular a medicamentos no vistos anteriormente.
L155: ##
L156: ### De la predicción al laboratorio
L157: 
L158: El estudio intentó además comprobar si algunas señales detectadas por el modelo tenían sentido biológico. Uno de los casos fue TYMS, una proteína que ProteinTalks relacionó con la respuesta a capecitabina. Cuando los investigadores redujeron experimentalmente la actividad de TYMS en células de cáncer de mama, estas se volvieron más sensibles al fármaco.
L159: cite96†Image: Una de las predicciones del modelo se llevó al laboratorio: al reducir la proteína TYMS, las células de cáncer de mama se volvieron más sensibles a la capecitabina.  L160: 
L161: Una de las predicciones del modelo se llevó al laboratorio: al reducir la proteína TYMS, las células de cáncer de mama se volvieron más sensibles a la capecitabina. Terceros
L162: Este tipo de prueba es especialmente importante porque una IA puede encontrar correlaciones sin identificar necesariamente la causa. Llevar una predicción al laboratorio permite comprobar si la proteína destacada participa realmente en la respuesta.
L163: ##
L164: ### También se probó con muestras de pacientes
L165: 
L166: Los investigadores fueron más allá de las líneas celulares. El trabajo incluye organoides derivados de pacientes y un análisis de biopsias de 501 personas con cáncer de mama triple negativo.
L167: 
L168: En esas muestras se analizaron 3.651 proteínas antes de la quimioterapia. Las puntuaciones generadas por el modelo consiguieron separar grupos de pacientes con diferentes resultados clínicos dentro de determinados tratamientos.
L169: Es una señal prometedora de que lo aprendido en cultivos celulares puede conservar cierta utilidad cuando se traslada a muestras humanas.
L170: 
L171: Pero todavía hay una diferencia enorme entre predecir retrospectivamente una respuesta y utilizar el sistema para decidir qué medicamento debe recibir una persona.
L172: ##
L173: ### Todavía no es un “oncólogo virtual”
L174: 
L175: ProteinTalks tampoco reproduce una célula completa. Trabaja principalmente con abundancia de proteínas y no captura toda la complejidad del tumor: modificaciones de esas proteínas, metabolismo, sistema inmunitario, microambiente tumoral o diferencias entre distintas células de una misma biopsia.
L176: Además, aún falta la prueba decisiva: un estudio prospectivo en el que el modelo recomiende tratamientos antes de administrarlos y se demuestre que esas decisiones mejoran los resultados de los pacientes.
L177: Por ahora, su mayor utilidad está un paso antes: reducir el número de fármacos y combinaciones que merece la pena llevar al laboratorio o estudiar en modelos derivados de pacientes. Si esa estrategia supera futuras validaciones clínicas, las “células virtuales” podrían convertirse en una herramienta para probar muchas opciones en el ordenador antes de escoger cuáles merece la pena probar en la realidad.

L21: cite10†ChatGPT†chat.openai.com cite11†Claude†claude.ai cite12†Perplexity†www.perplexity.ai cite13†Google AI†www.google.com L22: ## Key Takeaways
L23: 
L24:   * Between July 21 and July 22, at least 29 organizations fell victim to a malvertising campaign that led them to a malicious Claude Artifact publicly hosted on the legitimate cite14†Claude.ai†claude.ai domain.
L25: 
L26:   * The malicious Claude Artifact redirected users to an attacker-controlled domain, where they downloaded what looks like a legitimate Claude desktop app (`ClaudeDesktop.exe`). In reality, the executable led to the download of SectopRAT.
L27:   * The attackers used an array of anti-analysis techniques, including packaging the malware with VMProtect to make it difficult to reverse engineer and checking the graphics hardware on systems before deciding whether to actually execute the malicious payload as a way to suss out VMs. On Huntress' end, we used Claude to help wrangle with some of these analysis challenges during our investigation.
L28:   * We reported the malicious Claude Artifact to Anthropic; as of publication on July 22, the public Claude Artifact had been removed.
L29: 
L30: Update: We have updated the malware attribution for this blog to SectopRAT due to the presence of HVNC in the .NET payload after closer inspection of the related Command and Control services revealed in the Ethereum BSC transactions.
L31: ## Background
L32: 
L33: Between July 21 and July 22, 2026, Huntress' Security Operations Center (SOC) lit up with a swathe of unusual executable installs, Defender exclusions, and anomalous persistence across 29 organizations, all coming from `ClaudeDesktop.exe`. The attacks had one common denominator: victims had searched for the Claude desktop app and were taken to a malicious public Claude Artifact on the actual Claude AI domain, which appeared to be a legitimate download link for the desktop app.
L34: Our deeper investigation into the attacks revealed a frustrating anti-analysis technique, command-and-control (C2) data stored in the Ethereum blockchain, and at its core, SectopRAT, a remote access trojan (RAT) that siphons off user credit card data, personal information, files, and passwords.
L35: We have titled this campaign FakeAgent, for what we believe to be self-evident reasons: the use of Claude to host the malicious loader as a Claude Artifact, and the use of Claude Desktop itself as the masquerading application.
L36: On our end, the analysis of this attack was partially aided by Claude itself. Some reimplementation details, specifically regarding AES and SM5 emulation, were rolled out via Claude Opus 4.8. We think these details are important to disclose, for both transparency, and to be clear where LLM integrations give us an advantage as cyber defenders.
L37: ## Analysis
L38: ### Initial Access
L39: 
L40: cite15†SEO poisoning and malicious paid advertisements have been a thorn in the side of cybersecurity practitioners for some time now. This attack is no different. The user performed an innocuous Bing search for  "CLAUDE DESKTOP APP". As shown in Figure 1, the sponsored results were filled with fake pages pretending to offer Claude Desktop. However, mixed in with those results was a sponsored link to the legitimate cite14†Claude.ai†claude.ai domain.
L41: A closer look at that sponsored link showed something more sinister. Instead of sending the user to a normal page, the ad pointed to the public artifact hosted on cite14†Claude.ai†claude.ai . Public artifacts are documents or files that users or large language models can create, upload, and share publicly. They are often used to show simple proof-of-concept content, such as a one-page website, chart, or image.
L42: 
L43: cite16†Image†cdn.builder.io L44: Figure 1: Bing search results with several malicious sponsored advertisements, including the cite14†Claude.ai†claude.ai hosted public artifact.
L45: In this case, the victims are taken from Bing Search to a public artifact hosted at `claude[.]ai/public/artifacts/ca456f1f-44c0-42af-b329-4f1c7534a877`. Claude indicates in a disclaimer in Figure 2 that it posts across all its artifact pages: "Content is user-generated and unverified." We reported the artifact for takedown to help disrupt the distribution of this malware; it has since been removed by Anthropic.
L46: 
L47: However, before removal, the malicious artifact link had 7,100 page views.
L48: cite17†Image†cdn.builder.io L49: 
L50: Figure 2: Claude Desktop/Cowork phishing page hosted as a Claude artifact.
L51: 
L52: This user-generated artifact masquerades as a legitimate Claude Desktop installation, but redirects the user to an external domain when clicking the "Download" button. Specifically, they are sent to `claude.ai.download-app[.]us` (registered May 9, 2026) and subsequently to `downloading-api.it[.]com/html/claude/win`.
L53: At this point, the user is served with a malicious `ClaudeDesktop.exe` file, which they unknowingly download and execute, with disarmed trust given the legitimate cite14†Claude.ai†claude.ai domain they originally obtained it from.
L54: ### Into the Malware
L55: ### ClaudeDesktop.exe & DockerDesktop.exe
L56: 
L57: The primary executables are `ClaudeDesktop.exe` and `DockerDesktop.exe`. These are identical: one serves to download and stage the initial payload (`ClaudeDesktop.exe`) and the other (`DockerDesktop.exe`) is written to disk as a persistent scheduled task to repeatedly reinfect the computer.
L58: 
L59: cite18†Image†cdn.builder.io L60: 
L61: Figure 3: ClaudeDesktop.exe process details.
L62: It's worth noting that `ClaudeDesktop.exe` is not actually `ClaudeDesktop.exe`, but instead a component of JetBrains' `jcef_helper.exe`, a Chromium Embedded Framework application.
L63: 
L64: This application is vulnerable to a technique known as DLL sideloading.
L65: ### A brief aside on DLL sideloading
L66: 
L67: DLL sideloading is a technique whereby a malicious, tampered dynamically linked library (DLL) can be co-located within the search path of the application. These DLLs typically contain code that is imported and executed by the parent executable. By maliciously modifying that function in the DLL, an adversary can achieve execution in the context of a trusted and signed executable.
L68: With this in mind, our actual payload lives in the DLL that is located next to the malicious application (`libcef.dll`). This is a DLL typically found with the Chromium Embedded Framework (hence CEF) and by itself is not cause for alarm.
L69: 
L70: However, the hash for this file does not match public records, and thus, we can conclude that an adversary has likely tampered with it.
L71: 
L72: Upon examination of the `libcef.dll` binary, we note a few unique things about our malware:
L73:   * It's been packed with VMProtect, a commercial software protection tool that attackers have abused to make their malware notoriously difficult to reverse.
L74: 
L75:   * It has references to an Ethereum contract (`0xc1907d7be91f95903ad66d775c397302e7dd9228`)
L76: VMProtect is genuinely problematic as it makes malware analysis much slower and more resource-intensive for defenders, so we explore the Ethereum contract to begin with. In this case, the Ethereum contract referenced by the binary has no balance, but instead the function calls can be traced to ultimately downloading and executing a payload stored at `cache.dat`, which appears to subsequently install the secondary component of this malware, the RAT itself.
L77: This act of storing command-and-control information in the Ethereum blockchain is a known tactic called "EtherHiding" that has been taking malware development by storm. It is essentially a resilient command-and-control address: by simply posting a new transaction to the Ethereum address, an adversary can trivially rotate their command-and-control services in a manner that is difficult to take down or disrupt.
L78: The purpose of these Ethereum contracts is not to contain/move cryptocurrency funds, NFTs, or code representations of some transaction; but to provide a take-down resilient means to allow malware to shift its command and control service.
L79: By calling the Ethereum contract, we're given an encrypted response back, with no apparent way to decrypt it. Recursing through the binary, we can see that the application enters the VMProtect section shortly afterwards, and we're left with a dead end.
L80: What was the command and control? What details were being fetched from the Ethereum contract? Faced with the reality of having to work through VMProtect obfuscation or difficult dynamic analysis procedures, we move on to the other payload observed on the host.
L81: ### Unmasking the RAT
L82: 
L83: An additional persistence mechanism was written to `%APPDATA\Roaming\Microsoft\EdgeUpdate\Install\sslconf.exe`, so we can explore this next.
L84: 
L85: `Sslconf.exe` is once again a signed application—in this case, an IBM SPSS binary. IBM SPSS is a statistical analysis platform; so another legitimate and unremarkable application that's widely used in many verticals.
L86: However, our adversary is a fan of patterns. Upon further investigation, we found that the actor once again used DLL sideloading, this time via the sideloading vector  `tempdir.dll`. This file is also maliciously modified by the adversary, and this time it doesn't pack VMProtect.
